A radius is the straight-line distance from the center of a circle (or sphere) to any point on its edge.

Think of it this way: draw a dot in the middle of a piece of paper. That dot is the center. Now draw a circle around it. Any straight line you draw from that center dot to the edge of the circle — that line is a radius.

No matter which direction you draw that line, it will always be the same length. That is a key property: all radii of the same circle are equal in length.

To fully understand radius, you need to see how it connects to a few related measurements:

Diameter — If you draw a straight line that passes through the center and touches both sides of the circle, that line is the diameter. The diameter is simply twice the radius. So if the radius is 5 cm, the diameter is 10 cm. And conversely, the radius is always half the diameter.

Circumference — This is the total length of the boundary (the curved edge) of the circle. It equals 2 × π × radius (approximately 2 × 3.14159 × radius). The radius is the single most important input for calculating a circle's size.

Area — The space enclosed inside the circle equals π × radius². Again, the radius drives this calculation entirely.

So the radius is essentially the master measurement of a circle — know the radius, and you can figure out everything else about the circle.

The concept extends naturally into three dimensions. A sphere (like a ball) also has a radius: the distance from its center to any point on its surface. Everything works the same way — all radii of the same sphere are equal, and the radius determines the sphere's size completely.

The word is also used in ordinary conversation to mean the area within a certain distance from a central point — not strictly a geometric circle, but the idea is the same.

Examples:

  • "There are three hospitals within a 10-kilometre radius of the city center." — meaning within 10 km of that center point, in any direction.
  • "Please stay within a 500-metre radius of the campsite." — meaning don't go farther than 500 metres away from the campsite in any direction.

Here, "radius" describes a zone or region spreading outward equally in all directions from a fixed point. It is the most natural word for this idea because it comes directly from the geometric meaning.

There is a second, completely separate meaning of radius in anatomy. The radius is one of the two bones in your forearm — the part of your arm between your elbow and your wrist. The other bone is called the ulna.

The radius runs on the thumb side of your forearm. When your palm faces forward, it is the outer bone on the right arm and the outer bone on the left arm. It is slightly shorter than the ulna and is the bone primarily responsible for the rotation movement of your wrist — the motion you use when turning a door handle or screwing in a bottle cap.

This anatomical meaning is entirely distinct from the geometric one. They simply share the same word.

The plural of radius has two accepted forms:

  • Radii — the classical Latin plural (pronounced ray-dee-eye), widely used in mathematics and science.
  • Radiuses — the fully anglicised plural, equally correct and more common in everyday speech.

Both are standard. In academic or technical writing, radii is more common. In casual writing or speech, radiuses fits naturally.

ContextWhat "radius" means

In geometry, the radius is the distance from the center of a circle or sphere to its edge — the foundational measurement from which all other dimensions of that shape follow.

In everyday language, it describes the extent of a zone radiating equally in all directions from a central point.

In anatomy, it is the bone on the thumb side of the forearm.

The geometric sense is the original and most common meaning. The everyday figurative use flows directly from it. The anatomical use is a separate application of the same word, borrowed because the bone's position in the forearm somewhat resembles a spoke radiating from a wheel's center.
